deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It continues the meteorological register begun on the previous page (headed '1808 Jul. | Barometer auf 15° Wärme red. | Thermometer'). It covers 28–30 September and 1–21 October 1808.

Each row has the day number and then six columns:
- Columns 1–3: barometer readings at three times of day. These are excess lines (Paris lines) over 27 Paris inches, so a reading of 4,0 means 27 in 4,0 lines. They have been reduced to a standard temperature of 15°, probably on the Réaumur scale, though the scale is not named.
- Columns 4–6: thermometer readings at the same three times.

The reduction rule is stated on the previous page:
- at 28 in 0 lines, add 0.078 lines × (15° − c);
- at 27 in 6 lines, add 0.075 lines × (15° − c);
- equivalently, in units of 1/16 line, add 1.248 × (15° − c) and 1.200 × (15° − c).

Here c is the attached-thermometer reading. The factor is about 0.078/336 ≈ 1/4300 per degree, which is the relative mercury expansion per degree. My check: 0.078 × 16 = 1.248 and 0.075 × 16 = 1.200, so the restatement in sixteenths of a line is exact.

What the data show:
- Pressure lows on 29 September (27 in 1.3 lines at midday), 8 October (1.9) and around 17–19 October.
- A high on 4–5 October (about 27 in 11 lines).
- Temperatures falling from about 9–10° in late September and early October to about 2–5° by 19–21 October, consistent with Réaumur degrees in a Göttingen autumn.

No monthly means are computed on this page; the previous page has means for July and August only. The 21 October row is incomplete: the midday barometer and midday thermometer are blank, and the register stops there.

This is routine observational bookkeeping, presumably Gauss's own or copied by him, from his early Göttingen observatory period (1808). No derivation is present.

results.what: Daily barometer readings (reduced to 15°) and thermometer readings, three times a day, 28 Sep – 21 Oct 1808
results.modern_name: meteorological observation log; barometric temperature reduction to a standard temperature
results.usually_credited_to: standard practice of 18th/19th-century observatories (temperature correction of barometers via mercury expansion: Deluc and others)

deep.surprise_reason: Pure tabulated weather data with no mathematical content. Gauss is known to have kept meteorological and barometric records, and the temperature-reduction rule (from the previous page) is standard.

checkable.asserts: The reduction coefficient 0.078 line/degree equals 1.248 sixteenths of a line per degree (previous page, governs this table).
The reduction coefficient 0.075 line/degree equals 1.200 sixteenths of a line per degree.
